A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same pCQO-MIS research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable matching despite the title change and reorganization.

before.justification: v5 reports original MIS benchmark results, scalability experiments, parameter studies, and stationary-point analyses in Section 4 and Appendices C and E.

after.justification: v7 retains these original results and adds large-ER and BA evaluations, optimizer comparisons, and expanded clique-term ablations.

M1.justification: The clique-informed objective, projected momentum updates, degree-based initializations, MaxIS checking, and batch restart procedure remain unchanged. The new tuning description and local-search interpretation do not establish an algorithm change.

E1.justification: v7 adds Barabasi–Albert graphs across nine size/attachment configurations and extends evaluation to 3,000-node ER graphs with edge probabilities from 0.1 to 0.7 (Appendices E.2–E.3). These broaden the represented graph structures and large-graph scenarios while retaining SATLIB, earlier ER/GNM evaluations, and DIMACS.

E2.justification: New auxiliary comparisons introduce OnlineMIS on BA graphs (Table 5), MISB on DIMACS examples (Table 9), and vanilla GD in the optimizer study (Table 6). OnlineMIS and MISB scores are attributed to prior publications. The existing main benchmark comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include 30-second large-ER evaluations, BA evaluation selecting the best per-graph tuning result, matched-initialization GD/MGD comparisons, and 50-batch clique-term sweeps measuring solution size and steps to the first solution. BA runtime includes tuning and differs from the cited baselines' budgets. The original main benchmark settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v5's simple clique-removal comparison and parameter sweeps, v7 adds controlled GD-versus-MGD tests and systematic clique-on/off analyses across step sizes and edge penalties, including convergence-step results (Tables 6–8). The MIS-checking study is retained and moved from Appendix E.2 to Section 4.4, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report graph-averaged point estimates without repeated-run variability, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Additional graph counts and optimization batches do not introduce uncertainty-estimation practices.

E6.justification: Matched earlier tables retain their numerical results, but v7 adds substantial benchmark and ablation findings. Table 4 reports 76.5 versus ReduMIS's 61.5 and Gurobi's 55.6 for 3,000-node ER graphs at p=0.1 under the stated 30-second budget. Table 5 reports 111.75 versus ReduMIS's 116.88 for BA graphs with n=1000, q=50, under different budgets. These are additional comparisons, not version-to-version performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 2 corrects the extendability statement to apply to non-maximal independent sets, whereas v5 states it for independent sets generally. The theorem conditions and Appendix A arguments otherwise retain their mathematical substance; the new main-text proof sketches summarize existing proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same substantive claims: a dataless clique-informed formulation, local-minimizer and stationary-point characterizations, parallel momentum optimization, efficient checking, and competitive performance. New experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v7 interprets the restart procedure as a local-search heuristic in Remark 7. Appendix E.5 adds a conjecture that the clique term creates a smoother optimization landscape and acknowledges that some differently tuned configurations without that term might perform better. These add mechanism explanations and qualifications.

D1.justification: Where v5 provides fixed parameters and example grids, v7 specifies a two-stage tuning procedure with explicit ranges, initial T=750, subsequent iteration reduction, and approximate tuning cost (E.9.1). It clarifies one-graph tuning for each main dataset and adds hardware and tuning details for new experiments. The code pointer changes from a refactor branch to the repository root.

R1.justification: v7 adds Wu, Zhao, and Arora (2025), Barabasi and Albert (1999), and Singh and Govinda (2014), supporting BA evaluation and classical clique-solver comparisons. San Segundo et al. (2011) is removed. The broader related-work framework remains intact; bibliographic updates and consolidation of duplicate Ahn references do not add research coverage.

P1.justification: The title's word order changes, sentences are edited, and Section 3 gains brief proof sketches and explanatory remarks. The existing MIS-checking discussion moves into Section 4.4, Appendix E is reorganized, and acknowledgments are added. Most exposition and the overall narrative sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Six new tables substantially expand the benchmark and ablation displays. Retained tables receive revised rules, grouped headers, and highlighting of DIMACS shortfalls, while captions are enlarged. The earlier Figure 5 becomes main-text Figure 3; all five underlying graphics are retained.

improvement.justification: Compared with v5's simpler component comparison and example parameter grids, v7's controlled momentum and clique-term studies better support the design choices, while E.9.1 improves tuning documentation. New graph evaluations also expose performance shortfalls. The gains are useful but bounded: BA comparisons use unequal budgets, only five MISB examples are printed, and the main benchmark results and substantive proofs remain unchanged.
